questions.stem: Where is the supplied CLZ-180 web NSG associated?

options.B: A Windows VM's OS disk.
options.C: The web subnet.
options.D: The Azure subscription itself.

optionExplanations.A: Only web has the declared association.
optionExplanations.B: No VM or disk is declared.
optionExplanations.C: The association resource targets azurerm_subnet.web.
optionExplanations.D: NSGs attach to network boundaries, not this subscription scope.

questions.stem: Which custom NSG rule is evaluated first when several rules could match?

options.A: The rule with the longest name.
options.B: The matching rule with the highest number.
options.C: The newest rule regardless of priority.
options.D: The matching rule with the lowest priority number.

optionExplanations.A: Names do not determine evaluation order.
optionExplanations.B: That reverses the evaluation order.
optionExplanations.C: Creation time is not precedence.
optionExplanations.D: Azure evaluates increasing priority numbers.

questions.stem: What source does allow_admin_rdp use in this lesson?

options.B: Internet unconditionally.
options.C: VirtualNetwork only.
options.D: Every source through 0.0.0.0/0.

optionExplanations.A: The input supplies one administrator IPv4 /32.
optionExplanations.B: Internet is used for the HTTP teaching rule.
optionExplanations.C: That is not the supplied RDP source.
optionExplanations.D: The input rejects broad prefix lengths.

questions.stem: What should the documented plan using admin_cidr=0.0.0.0/0 demonstrate?

options.B: Input rejection before Azure is changed.
options.C: Removal of the VNet.
options.D: A quota increase.

optionExplanations.A: A failed plan does not apply changes.
optionExplanations.B: The validation requires a /32.
optionExplanations.C: Planning does not destroy this module merely from invalid input.
optionExplanations.D: CIDR validation is not quota management.

questions.stem: A private IPv4 /32 passes this source's admin_cidr validation. What does passing actually prove?

options.A: The address is guaranteed publicly routable.
options.B: The address belongs to the current learner.
options.C: IPv4 CIDR shape and /32 prefix length, not public routability.
options.D: A Windows VM is reachable from it.

optionExplanations.A: The syntax checks cannot prove that.
optionExplanations.B: No ownership query is implemented.
optionExplanations.C: The code does not classify public versus private ranges.
optionExplanations.D: This lesson has no VM and the validator does not test connectivity.

questions.stem: Which destination port does allow_http admit from Internet?

options.B: UDP 53
options.C: TCP 1433
options.D: TCP 80

optionExplanations.A: That is the scoped administration port.
optionExplanations.B: No DNS allow rule is declared.
optionExplanations.C: No SQL allow rule is declared.
optionExplanations.D: This is the deliberately public HTTP teaching rule.

questions.stem: A learner adds a rule at priority 90. Why is it unsuitable as a normal custom NSG rule?

options.B: Every priority must be a multiple of 100.
options.C: Priority is a free-form string.
options.D: Only three rules are permitted.

optionExplanations.A: Custom priorities range from 100 through 4096.
optionExplanations.B: That is not required.
optionExplanations.C: It is a numeric value.
optionExplanations.D: The lesson has three, but that is not the NSG limit.

questions.stem: Two inbound rules are assigned priority 110. What should be corrected?

options.A: Rename both rules to the same name.
options.B: Give each inbound rule a unique priority.
options.C: Change only the Project tag.
options.D: Add a Windows VM first.

optionExplanations.A: That creates another conflict.
optionExplanations.B: Priorities must be unique for rules in the same direction.
optionExplanations.C: Tags do not control rule priority.
optionExplanations.D: Compute does not resolve rule conflicts.

questions.stem: Why does the lesson include deny_other_rdp at priority 120 after the administrator allow at 110?

options.A: To block the allowed administrator before 110.
options.B: To enable SQL access.
options.C: To deny other matching RDP sources after the allowed /32 is considered.
options.D: To create a new public IP.

optionExplanations.A: 120 is evaluated later.
optionExplanations.B: The rule targets RDP, not SQL.
optionExplanations.C: Lower-numbered allow is considered first.
optionExplanations.D: NSG rules do not provision public addresses.

questions.stem: Does allowing TCP 80 in CLZ-180 prove an HTTP service is running?

options.B: Only if the rule name says http.
options.C: Yes; every subnet hosts a web listener.
options.D: No; a rule permits traffic but does not deploy a server.

optionExplanations.A: They do not install application services.
optionExplanations.B: Names do not install software.
optionExplanations.C: Subnets do not imply application processes.
optionExplanations.D: There is no VM or IIS resource in this lesson.

questions.stem: An inbound connection is allowed by an NSG. How is its response traffic normally treated?

options.A: The NSG tracks the flow and permits its response.
options.B: A mirrored response rule is always mandatory.
options.C: All outbound traffic becomes permanently allowed.
options.D: The NSG forwards traffic without any flow checks.

optionExplanations.A: NSG rules are stateful.
optionExplanations.B: Stateful tracking normally handles return traffic.
optionExplanations.C: Only the tracked flow gains response handling.
optionExplanations.D: Stateful filtering still applies.

questions.stem: Which validation output matters for CLZ-180's administrator access?

options.A: Only the NSG resource's provisioning state.
options.B: The actual rule's source, destination port, priority, and access.
options.C: Only the Terraform binary size.
options.D: Only the number of subnets.

optionExplanations.A: Succeeded does not by itself prove every intended rule value.
optionExplanations.B: These establish the intended scoped filter.
optionExplanations.C: Binary size does not show Azure policy.
optionExplanations.D: Subnet count does not verify source, port, action, and priority.

questions.stem: Why replace the default 203.0.113.10/32 before a real direct-access lesson?

options.A: It is always the learner's Azure gateway.
options.B: The prefix length is invalid.
options.C: It is an example address, not evidence of the learner's public source.
options.D: Terraform automatically discovers the browser IP.

optionExplanations.A: No such assignment is guaranteed.
optionExplanations.B: /32 is the required length.
optionExplanations.C: Use the current actual public IPv4.
optionExplanations.D: No discovery is implemented in this input.

questions.stem: Which production pattern reduces direct Internet RDP exposure?

options.B: Rename the RDP rule secure.
options.C: Rely on the Environment tag.
options.D: Bastion, VPN, or another approved private management path.

optionExplanations.A: That broadens exposure.
optionExplanations.B: Names do not restrict traffic.
optionExplanations.C: Tags are not packet filters.
optionExplanations.D: The production delta replaces direct public administration.

questions.stem: An administrator source matches allow_admin_rdp at 110 and deny_other_rdp at 120. What is the result?

options.A: The allow at 110 is matched first.
options.B: Both rules are merged into a random outcome.
options.C: The later deny always overrides every allow.
options.D: The connection is allowed only on port 80.

optionExplanations.A: Processing stops at the first matching rule.
optionExplanations.B: Evaluation is deterministic.
optionExplanations.C: Order is by priority, not universal deny preference.
optionExplanations.D: This question concerns the TCP 3389 rules.

questions.stem: A new matching RDP deny is added at priority 105. What happens to the allow at 110 for that traffic?

options.B: The 105 deny wins first.
options.C: Both cancel and create a public IP.
options.D: Azure sorts by rule names instead.

optionExplanations.A: The lower-numbered match wins.
optionExplanations.B: Its lower priority number gives precedence.
optionExplanations.C: Rules do not create addresses.
optionExplanations.D: Priorities determine order.

questions.learningObjective: Reject IPv6 in the scoped input
questions.stem: Why would admin_cidr=2001:db8::1/128 fail this lesson's validator?

options.B: IPv6 can be used only as a tag.
options.C: It requires an IPv4 address and /32 length.
options.D: The default VM size disallows all IPs.

optionExplanations.A: That broader claim is false.
optionExplanations.B: IPv6 is a network protocol, not merely metadata.
optionExplanations.C: The colon and prefix checks exclude this IPv6 input.
optionExplanations.D: No VM size is part of this lesson.

questions.stem: Later RDP remains unreachable despite a correct NSG rule. What else must be checked?

options.B: Whether local.tags contains a password.
options.C: Whether the NSG has the longest name.
options.D: A real public, NAT, or Bastion ingress path and running workload.

optionExplanations.A: Titles do not provide a network path.
optionExplanations.B: Secrets do not belong in tags.
optionExplanations.C: Name length is not connectivity.
optionExplanations.D: Filtering permission alone does not create reachability.

questions.stem: After custom rules, which Azure default commonly denies other unsolicited inbound traffic?

options.B: A hidden allow for every public source.
options.C: ManagedBy=Terraform at priority 1.
options.D: A README Cleanup heading.

optionExplanations.A: Default rules include a low-precedence final deny.
optionExplanations.B: There is no universal public inbound allow.
optionExplanations.C: Tags are not NSG rules.
optionExplanations.D: Markdown does not filter packets.

questions.stem: The allow_http rule uses Internet as its source. What is Internet here?

options.A: The name of this lesson's subnet.
options.B: An Azure service tag representing that source category.
options.C: A VM's local administrator account.
options.D: A Terraform provider alias.

optionExplanations.A: The subnet is web-snet.
optionExplanations.B: It is not a generated password or resource.
optionExplanations.C: No such account is declared here.
optionExplanations.D: It is a network rule source value.

questions.stem: In allow_http, source_port_range is * and destination_port_range is 80. Why?

options.A: The server must listen on every port.
options.B: Both fields always mean the VM's port.
options.C: Clients may use different source ports to reach HTTP port 80.
options.D: It permits only outbound DNS.

optionExplanations.A: Wildcard source ports do not open every destination.
optionExplanations.B: Source and destination have distinct roles.
optionExplanations.C: Destination is the service port.
optionExplanations.D: The rule is inbound TCP HTTP.

questions.stem: Why read Azure NSG rules after apply instead of relying only on terraform validate?

options.B: Azure tags replace rule readback.
options.C: A saved pre-apply plan is always proof of the live rule set.
options.D: Readback checks the deployed rule values.

optionExplanations.A: It does not apply changes.
optionExplanations.B: Tags are different metadata.
optionExplanations.C: The actual Azure configuration can differ until apply and readback.
optionExplanations.D: Static validity is not proof of actual applied policy.

questions.stem: CLZ-180 follows CLZ-170. Does it attach rules to CLZ-170's live VNet by navigation alone?

options.A: No; it recreates its own independent network.
options.B: Yes; the next lesson imports automatically.
options.C: Only if names look similar.
options.D: Yes; prerequisites share one global state.

optionExplanations.A: The source declares the VNet and subnets again.
optionExplanations.B: Navigation does not invoke import.
optionExplanations.C: Similar names do not link state ownership.
optionExplanations.D: Standalone lesson folders keep separate contexts.

questions.stem: The NSG is associated with web-snet. Which future workload NICs are affected by that subnet filter?

options.B: NICs placed in that subnet.
options.C: Only NICs whose names contain web.
options.D: Only NICs with an HTTP tag.

optionExplanations.A: The association is not global.
optionExplanations.B: Subnet-associated rules apply to traffic of its attached workloads.
optionExplanations.C: Attachment, not name substring, determines coverage.
optionExplanations.D: Tags do not define the association.

questions.stem: Why might production use Application Security Groups in NSG rules?

options.B: To create subscription RBAC assignments.
options.C: To group workload interfaces by application intent.
options.D: To remove all route tables automatically.

optionExplanations.A: ASGs are network policy grouping constructs.
optionExplanations.B: RBAC is separate.
optionExplanations.C: This can simplify rules based on roles.
optionExplanations.D: They do not delete routing infrastructure.

questions.stem: Which change would weaken CLZ-180's administrator rule?

options.A: Changing a safe /32 to another verified safe /32.
options.B: Reading rule properties with Azure CLI.
options.C: Adding a nonsecret Owner tag.
options.D: Changing the RDP source to a broad network.

optionExplanations.A: That updates the intended administrator source.
optionExplanations.B: Inspection does not widen access.
optionExplanations.C: Metadata does not broaden the rule.
optionExplanations.D: It grants access to more source addresses.

questions.stem: What is directly billed for the NSG and its rules in this lesson?

options.B: One Windows license per rule.
options.C: One VM hour per priority number.
options.D: A mandatory Bastion instance.

optionExplanations.A: Traffic and later workloads may introduce costs.
optionExplanations.B: Rules are not operating systems.
optionExplanations.C: Priorities are not compute capacity.
optionExplanations.D: Bastion is not deployed here.

questions.learningObjective: Use effective rules when layers exist
questions.stem: If a later VM has both subnet and NIC NSGs, how should connectivity be diagnosed?

options.A: Only the rule with the shortest name matters.
options.B: Evaluate the effective rules across both associations.
options.C: Only the NIC NSG applies; subnet rules vanish.
options.D: The Project tag bypasses both NSGs.

optionExplanations.A: Names do not choose the effective filter.
optionExplanations.B: Traffic must be permitted through the relevant layers.
optionExplanations.C: Both can affect the traffic.
optionExplanations.D: Tags do not bypass rules.

questions.stem: What confirms successful CLZ-180 cleanup at the group boundary?

options.A: The rule query alone returns no results.
options.B: The plan file is renamed.
options.C: Destroy finishes and Azure reports the named group absent.
options.D: RDP stops responding from one source.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong context or filtering can also hide results.
optionExplanations.B: That does not delete Azure resources.
optionExplanations.C: Its independently declared network/NSG belong to that disposable boundary.
optionExplanations.D: Connectivity failure is not deletion proof.

sources.title: Manage resource groups with Azure CLI

questions.stem: The learner's public IP changes after moving networks. What is the intended remediation?

options.B: Disable all NSGs permanently.
options.C: Put the new IP in ManagedBy only.
options.D: Update admin_cidr to the current public IPv4 /32 and review the plan.

optionExplanations.A: The safety validation rejects that broad range.
optionExplanations.B: That removes the teaching protection.
optionExplanations.C: A tag does not update source_address_prefix.
optionExplanations.D: Keep administration narrowly scoped.
